messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: abs(x) is evil, but what about sqrt(square(x))?
parts:
Hi,
 
I come across to calculate in some models the variance of x, and put into normal(mu,sigma),
so I have the expression sqrt(square(x)) which I could write also as abs(x) in which the
manual shows a warning. 

But what about sqrt(square(x)) which sounds silly, but is it advantageous to abs(x) in STAN?

Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] abs(x) is evil, but what about sqrt(square(x))?
parts:
:-) Insofar as Stan does the right thing with functions
and derivatives, sqrt(square(x)) is just a less efficient
way to implement abs(x).

Not being differentiable at 0 can be a problem in that
neighborhood with the Hamiltonian simulation, but the
bigger issue is the multimodality typically introduced
by the symmetry around 0 making p(x, ...) = p(-x, ...).
It's a classic case of non-identifiability.

- Bob

> I come across to calculate in some models the variance of x, and put into normal(mu,sigma),
> so I have the expression sqrt(square(x)) which I could write also as abs(x) in which the

> manual shows are warning.

Folk theorem warning — I’m willing to bet that a model which requires an empirical
variance of parameters is misspecified. For example, you might really want to
model the population with a hierarchical model.

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] abs(x) is evil, but what about sqrt(square(x))?
parts:
Dear Michael,

ARMA-GARCH Models require the variance, Where do
you see a miss specification?
We need to take the sqrt, since normal() in STAN requires the
stddev. 

Andre

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] abs(x) is evil, but what about sqrt(square(x))?
parts:
Yeah, but if you’re doing ARMA on the variance then you wouldn’t need
the square, unless you’re allowing the ARMA coefficients to be negative
in which case you have some serious modeling problems.  This is a nice
example where it doesn’t make much sense to put an ARMA structure on
the constrained space but rather on an unconstrained latent space, i.e.
log(variance) or log(standard deviation).  Folk theorem in action.

Michael, when phi < 0, we get alternating series, in what way would that 
affect STAN negatively?

   sigma[t] <- sqrt(alpha[1]
                     + alpha[2] * square(err[t-1])
                     + alpha[3] * square(sigma[t-1]));

would then?

   sigma[t] <- log(alpha[1]
                     + alpha[2] * exp(err[t-1])
                     + alpha[3] * exp(sigma[t-1]));

Anyway your idea sounds reasonable for phi > 0.

Andre
